title: Bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng
creator: chinese-bronze-casters
location: Hubei Provincial Museum, Wuhan (excavated at Suizhou, 1978)
note: Sixty-five tuned bronze bells on a three-tier frame, each sounding two pitches, the greatest musical find of ancient China.
description: When the tomb of Marquis Yi, ruler of the small state of Zeng, was excavated at Suizhou in Hubei in 1978, archaeologists found a ritual orchestra laid out as if for a performance: stone chimes, zithers, mouth organs, flutes, drums and, along two walls of the central chamber, a set of sixty-five bronze bells hung on an L-shaped lacquered wooden frame supported by bronze figures of warriors. The bells weigh over two and a half tonnes in all and span about five octaves. Almond-shaped in cross-section, each produces two distinct notes when struck at the centre or the side, and gold-inlaid inscriptions name these pitches and their equivalents in the systems of other states, revealing a sophisticated theory of absolute pitch and transposition. The set was dated by a bell given by the King of Chu in 433 BC. Still playable, it has been reproduced and recorded, and was used in the music for the Hong Kong handover in 1997. The bells are also treated as a masterpiece of bronze casting in the art section.
image_file: 湖北博物館曾侯乙編鐘.jpg
image_caption: The bells on their bronze-and-lacquer frame, Hubei Provincial Museum

title: Solitary Orchid (Jieshi diao: Youlan)
creator: qiu-gongming
location: Manuscript in the Tokyo National Museum
note: The oldest surviving score of Chinese music, a qin piece written out in words in a Tang manuscript preserved in Japan.
description: Solitary Orchid in the Stone Tablet Mode survives in a single handwritten scroll copied in Tang China, probably in the seventh century, and kept for over a millennium in Japan, where it is now in the Tokyo National Museum. Its preface credits the piece to Qiu Gongming of the sixth century. Unlike later qin tablature, which uses abbreviated composite characters, the score describes every action in full sentences: which finger stops which string at which stud, how to pluck, slide and ornament. Rhythm is not shown, so the music must be reconstructed by interpretation, and several modern players have recorded versions. The title evokes the image of a noble orchid growing unseen, which tradition associates with Confucius lamenting that his talents went unrecognised. The manuscript is a unique witness to early qin technique and is registered as a National Treasure of Japan.
image_caption: Opening of the Tang manuscript, written out in words, Tokyo National Museum

title: Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute (Hujia shiba pai)
creator: cai-yan
year: attributed late 2nd century; qin versions Ming
location: Qin handbooks from the 15th century onward
note: A cycle of eighteen laments in the voice of Cai Yan, captive among the Xiongnu, sung to the qin and painted many times.
description: The Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute is a sequence of poems in which Cai Yan tells of her capture by the Xiongnu, her years in the north, her two sons, and her heartbreak at leaving them when she was ransomed back to China. The word pai suggests a 'beat' or stanza, and the 'nomad flute' (hujia) is the reed pipe of the steppe whose sound haunts her. The attribution to Cai Yan herself is doubted by most modern scholars, who date the poem to the Tang or later; it first appears in a Song anthology. Qin pieces with the same title, of which several versions survive in Ming handbooks, set or evoke the cycle, and the story was a favourite subject of painters from the Song onward, with famous handscrolls illustrating its eighteen scenes. It remains one of the most expressive works of the qin repertory.
image_file: 宋 佚名 胡笳十八拍 文姬歸漢圖 卷-Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute- The Story of Lady Wenji MET DP213003 CRD.jpg
image_caption: Scene from a handscroll illustrating the Eighteen Songs, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Guangling san
creator: ji-kang
location: Earliest score in the Shenqi mipu (1425)
note: The longest and most dramatic qin piece, about the assassin Nie Zheng, legendary as the music Ji Kang played before his death.
description: Guangling san (Melody of Guangling) was already famous in the third century, when Ji Kang is said to have played it at his execution in 262 and lamented that no one would now learn it. The piece is not Ji Kang's composition: he is said to have learned it from a mysterious stranger, and its origins are unknown. A version survived, and was printed in 1425 in Zhu Quan's Shenqi mipu, with forty-five sections whose titles tell the story of Nie Zheng, who avenged his father by assassinating the King of Han, then disfigured himself to protect his family. The music is unusually vigorous and dramatic for the qin, using the low strings forcefully. Guan Pinghu's reconstruction of the 1425 tablature in the 1950s brought it back into performance, and it is regarded as one of the summits of the qin repertory.

title: Music Has in It Neither Grief nor Joy (Sheng wu aile lun)
creator: ji-kang
note: Ji Kang's dialogue arguing that sound has no emotion of its own, a radical challenge to the Confucian theory of music.
description: Confucian tradition, expressed in the Record of Music in the Book of Rites, held that music arises from feeling and shapes the moral character of the listener and the state. In this essay, written as a debate between a host and a guest from Qin, Ji Kang argues instead that sounds are simply harmonious or not, like flavours, and that grief and joy belong to the listener's mind, which is merely stirred by music to express what it already holds. The argument draws on Daoist ideas of naturalness and on the logic of 'pure conversation' (qingtan) popular in his circle. It is the most sophisticated piece of musical aesthetics from early China and is often compared with Western debates about whether music expresses emotion.

title: High Mountains and Flowing Water (Gaoshan liushui)
creator: guqin-masters
location: Earliest score in the Shenqi mipu (1425)
note: Qin music on the legend of Boya and his friend Zhong Ziqi, the 'one who knew his sound'; Flowing Water travelled on the Voyager Golden Record.
description: The Liezi tells of the qin player Boya, whose friend Zhong Ziqi understood exactly what he was thinking as he played, saying 'how lofty, like Mount Tai' or 'how vast, like rivers'. When Zhong died, Boya broke his strings and never played again, and zhiyin, 'one who knows the sound', became the Chinese word for a true friend. In the Shenqi mipu of 1425 the music appears as a pair of pieces, High Mountains and Flowing Water, and later handbooks expanded them. The version of Flowing Water from the nineteenth-century Sichuan school, with its famous passage of rolling and sliding imitating rushing water, was played by Guan Pinghu in a recording chosen for the Voyager Golden Record in 1977. A guzheng piece of the same name is a different work.
image_caption: A guqin of the Zhongni shape

title: Plum Blossom Three Variations (Meihua sannong)
creator: guqin-masters
location: Earliest score in the Shenqi mipu (1425)
note: A qin piece on the plum, which blossoms in winter, with a refrain played three times in harmonics.
description: The piece is traditionally derived from a flute melody played by the Eastern Jin general Huan Yi, but the first score is in the Shenqi mipu of 1425. Its name comes from a refrain repeated three times, each time at a different position on the instrument, in the bell-like harmonics of the qin, evoking plum blossoms that defy the cold. The plum, flowering at the end of winter, symbolised integrity in adversity, and the piece became one of the most popular in the repertory, also arranged for the xiao flute and other instruments.

title: Shenqi mipu
creator: zhu-quan
note: The earliest surviving printed handbook of qin music, preserving 64 pieces including Guangling san.
description: Prince Zhu Quan compiled the Handbook of Mysterious and Marvellous Secrets over twelve years and printed it in 1425. Its first volume, the 'Pieces from Remote Antiquity', preserves music he regarded as handed down from the Song and earlier, including Guangling san, Flowing Water and Plum Blossom, while later volumes contain more recent pieces. Each piece has a short preface about its origins and is written in the reduced tablature (jianzi pu) of qin notation, which combines parts of characters to show string, finger and stud. As the oldest large collection, it is the main source for reconstructions of early qin music and is the starting point for almost every history of the instrument.
image_caption: A page of qin tablature from the Shenqi mipu

title: Twelve-tone equal temperament (Yuelü quanshu)
creator: zhu-zaiyu
note: The first exact published calculation of the equal division of the octave into twelve semitones.
description: Chinese theorists had long generated the twelve pitches by the 'add and subtract a third' method, the equivalent of the Pythagorean cycle of fifths, which never quite returns to its starting point. In his New Account of the Science of Pitch-pipes (Lülü jingyi), finished in 1584 and gathered in the Yuelü quanshu, Zhu Zaiyu solved the problem by making each semitone the ratio of the twelfth root of two, which he calculated to twenty-five digits using a large abacus. He described pipes and strings built to these proportions and applied the system to the qin and ritual music. His work was hardly used in Chinese practice, but it is a landmark in the history of tuning; whether knowledge of it reached Europe, where Simon Stevin and Marin Mersenne worked on the same problem, is uncertain.
image_caption: Dance diagram from Zhu Zaiyu's writings on music and dance

title: Dance of the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Garment (Nishang yuyi qu)
creator: tang-xuanzong
note: The most famous Tang court dance suite, said to have been arranged by Xuanzong and danced by Yang Guifei.
description: According to legend Emperor Xuanzong composed this music after dreaming of a visit to the palace of the moon, but historical sources suggest he adapted an Indian-derived Brahman melody presented by a frontier governor. It was a large suite (daqu) in many sections, beginning with free-rhythm preludes and building to a fast dance, performed by richly costumed dancers, among them Xuanzong's consort Yang Guifei. After the An Lushan rebellion it came to symbolise the lost splendour of the Kaiyuan era, and Bai Juyi's 'Song of Everlasting Regret' made it an emblem of the doomed love story. The music was lost, though the Southern Tang queen Zhou Ehuang and the Song poet Jiang Kui each claimed to have recovered parts of it. It lives on in poetry, painting and kunqu, notably in The Palace of Eternal Youth.

title: Pear Garden (Liyuan)
creator: tang-xuanzong
note: The court academy of music and performance where Xuanzong trained musicians himself; Chinese actors still call themselves its disciples.
description: In 714 Xuanzong selected some three hundred musicians and several hundred palace women to study the new 'law music' (faqu) in the Pear Garden of the palace, where he personally corrected their mistakes. The academy formed part of a larger reorganisation of court music that also created teaching offices (jiaofang) for popular music. The Pear Garden was devastated by the An Lushan rebellion, but its name passed to the whole profession of theatre: actors became 'disciples of the Pear Garden' (liyuan dizi), and Xuanzong was worshipped by them as a patron deity. Its fame illustrates the high prestige of music at the Tang court, at a time when Chang'an drew performers from across Asia.

title: Five-stringed pipa of the Shōsōin
creator: tang-court-musicians
note: The only surviving five-string pipa of the Tang period, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, deposited at Tōdai-ji in 756.
description: The Shōsōin, the storehouse of Tōdai-ji in Nara, holds the treasures that Empress Kōmyō dedicated in 756 after the death of Emperor Shōmu, among them some of the finest musical instruments of the eighth century. This lute of red sandalwood has five strings and a straight neck, an Indian and Central Asian form, as opposed to the four-string bent-necked pipa that survived in Chinese and Japanese music. Its body is inlaid with mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell, and its plectrum guard shows a Central Asian musician riding a camel and playing the pipa among tropical trees. It is generally thought to have been made in Tang China. Together with the Shōsōin's harps, zithers and ruan, it shows the cosmopolitan instruments of the Tang court, and it is shown only occasionally at the annual exhibition in Nara.
image_file: 模造螺鈿紫檀五弦琵琶の正面.jpg
image_caption: Modern replica of the Shōsōin five-string pipa with its mother-of-pearl decoration

title: Ruan (genkan) of the Shōsōin
creator: tang-court-musicians
note: A round-bodied Tang lute decorated with a scene of figures playing music, the best-preserved early ruan.
description: The ruan, a lute with a round body and long neck named after Ruan Xian, one of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, was played at the Tang court. The Shōsōin keeps one decorated with mother-of-pearl inlay and a painted leather plectrum guard showing figures under trees. Such instruments disappeared from Japanese music but are a key source for reconstructions of Tang instruments, and the modern Chinese orchestra uses several sizes of ruan revived in the twentieth century.
image_caption: The Shōsōin storehouse at Tōdai-ji, Nara, where the instrument is kept

title: Dunhuang pipa scores
creator: tang-court-musicians
note: Twenty-five pieces in pipa tablature found in the Dunhuang library cave, the largest surviving source of Tang-period music.
description: Among the manuscripts sealed in Cave 17 at Dunhuang around 1000 and taken to Paris by Paul Pelliot in 1908 is a scroll whose back carries twenty-five short pieces in a tablature for the four-string pipa, copied around 933. They include tunes with names like 'Qingbei yue' and 'Xiliang yue', related to the banquet music of the late Tang and Five Dynasties. The tablature shows string and fret, but how to read the rhythm marks has been fiercely debated since the 1930s, and Chinese, Japanese and British scholars, notably Laurence Picken and his Cambridge group, have produced very different transcriptions with the help of Japanese gagaku scores. The manuscript is the main written witness to the court music of Tang China.

title: The Prince of Qin Breaks the Ranks (Qinwang pozhen yue)
creator: tang-court-musicians
location: Tang court; survives in Japan as Ōdai hajin raku
note: A Tang military dance celebrating Li Shimin's victories, which survives only through Japanese gagaku.
description: Composed to celebrate the victories of Li Shimin, Prince of Qin, who became Emperor Taizong in 626, this was performed at the Tang court by large numbers of armoured dancers with banners and drums. Xuanzang reports that Indian kings asked him about it. The music was later lost in China but was transmitted to Japan, where a gagaku piece called Ōdai hajin raku survives in tablature and performance, much slowed. It illustrates how much Tang music survives only in its Japanese afterlife.

title: Dasheng bells (Dasheng bianzhong)
creator: huizong
location: Surviving bells in the Palace Museum, Beijing, Liaoning Provincial Museum and elsewhere
note: Bells cast for Huizong's revival of ancient ritual music, modelled on a Zhou bell; some were later sent to Korea.
description: In 1104 Huizong set up a bureau to create new ritual music, the Dasheng yue (Music of Great Brilliance), on the basis of ancient models. Its centrepiece was a new series of bronze bells cast in 1105, modelled on six ancient bells said to have been found at Yingtian, and inscribed with their pitch names. The project expressed the Song belief that correct music would bring cosmic harmony and a prosperous state. When the Jurchen took Kaifeng in 1127 the bells were carried north and later reused by Jin and Yuan courts; dozens survive today. In 1116 Huizong had sent a complete set of ritual instruments and music to the Goryeo king of Korea, the origin of Korean aak.

title: Songs of the Whitestone Taoist (Baishi daoren gequ)
creator: jiang-kui
location: Printed in the Qing from Song editions (1743)
note: Seventeen ci songs with melodies in Song notation, the only large body of Song song to survive.
description: Jiang Kui's songbook contains lyrics he wrote to his own melodies, together with ritual and qin songs, and above each syllable is a sign in the 'popular notation' (suzi pu) used by Song musicians. The collection was rediscovered and reprinted in the eighteenth century, and since the twentieth century scholars, including Yang Yinliu and Laurence Picken, have decoded the notation and produced transcriptions, though questions of rhythm remain open. The songs include 'Dark Fragrance' (Anxiang) and 'Sparse Shadows' (Shuying), written in 1191 on the plum blossom for his patron Fan Chengda, and 'Yangzhou Slow Song' (Yangzhou man), mourning a city ruined by war. They are the only examples of how the ci of the Song, normally known only as poetry, actually sounded.

title: The Single Sword Meeting (Dandao hui)
creator: guan-hanqing
note: A Yuan zaju about the hero Guan Yu, still performed as a kunqu and opera scene.
description: In this historical zaju, Lu Su of Wu invites Guan Yu to a banquet in order to force the return of Jingzhou, but Guan Yu crosses the river with only a single sword and so overawes his hosts that he returns unharmed. The fourth act contains the famous arias sung by Guan Yu as he crosses the Yangtze, looking back on the battle of the Red Cliffs and the blood of heroes in the river. The scene survived on the kunqu stage as 'Dao hui' and was taken into Peking opera, keeping Guan Hanqing's words alive in performance for seven centuries.

title: Kunqu (the water-mill style)
creator: wei-liangfu
note: The slow, refined singing of Kunshan, developed by Wei Liangfu and his circle, which became the classical opera of China.
description: Kunqu takes its name from the town of Kunshan near Suzhou, one of several local styles for singing southern drama in the Ming. In the mid sixteenth century Wei Liangfu and fellow musicians refined it into a style in which every syllable is sung with its correct tone and articulated in three parts, head, belly and tail, with gracefully ornamented melody over the dizi flute. Because each word is drawn out like water from a mill, it was called shuimo diao. The playwright Liang Chenyu wrote Washing Silk for it, and within a few decades kunqu became the elite theatre of the empire, performed by household troupes of the rich and by professional companies. Its dance, gesture and role types fed into almost every later regional opera. Kunqu declined in the nineteenth century but was saved by a Suzhou school of actors in the 1920s, and in 2001 it was among the first items proclaimed by UNESCO as Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
image_caption: A kunqu performance in Taipei

title: The Peony Pavilion (in kunqu performance)
creator: tang-xianzu
location: Linchuan; staged across Jiangnan from c. 1600
note: Tang Xianzu's play of love beyond death, the heart of the kunqu repertory, especially the scenes 'Wandering in the Garden' and 'Interrupted Dream'.
description: Tang Xianzu's fifty-five-scene chuanqi tells of Du Liniang, who falls in love with a young man in a dream, pines away and dies, and is brought back to life by her love. Within a few decades it was being sung to kunqu melodies, and editors adjusted its text to fit the rules of the music, which Tang resented. On the stage it lives mainly in excerpts (zhezixi), above all 'Wandering in the Garden, Interrupted Dream' (Youyuan jingmeng), in which the dan heroine, with fan and long sleeves, discovers the spring garden and her own longing. Mei Lanfang and later kunqu stars made these scenes famous, and modern productions have staged the whole play over several nights, including Bai Xianyong's 'Young Lovers' version of 2004 and Peter Sellars's Western adaptation of 1998. The play as literature is treated in the literature section.
image_caption: Page from an early edition of The Peony Pavilion (Mudan ting huanhun ji)

title: The Palace of Eternal Youth (Changsheng dian)
creator: hong-sheng
note: Hong Sheng's fifty-scene kunqu drama on Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, admired for its musical craft.
description: Hong Sheng retold the love of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, the An Lushan rebellion and her forced death at Mawei, and the lovers' final reunion in the palace of the moon, drawing on Bai Juyi's 'Song of Everlasting Regret' and Bai Pu's Yuan play Rain on the Paulownia Tree. Completed in 1688 after more than a decade of revision, it was admired for the musical correctness of its arias, which were set with the help of the musician Xu Lin. A performance in 1689 during the mourning period for the empress dowager led to Hong Sheng's ruin, but the play remained popular, and scenes such as 'The Dance of the Rainbow Skirt' and 'Bidding Farewell to the Grave' are still standards of kunqu.
image_file: The Hall of Everlasting Life (CBL J 2809).jpg
image_caption: The Hall of Everlasting Life, Chester Beatty Library, Dublin

title: Etenraku
creator: imperial-household-gagaku
location: Imperial court, Kyoto; today the Imperial Household Agency, Tokyo
note: The best-known piece of Japanese court music, a slow tōgaku melody in the hyōjō mode.
description: Etenraku, 'music of the heavens', belongs to the tōgaku repertory of Chinese origin, though its exact source is uncertain and some accounts credit Japanese courtiers with its composition. It is played by the full gagaku ensemble: the hichiriki oboe and ryūteki flute carry the melody, the shō mouth organ sustains clusters of tones, the biwa and koto mark the beats with broken chords and patterns, and the kakko, taiko and shōko drums frame each phrase. The pace is very slow and the texture shimmering, the result of centuries of gradual slowing of what was probably once lively banquet music. It exists in versions in three modes, and in the Edo period its melody was sung as the popular song 'Etenraku imayō' and adapted in koto music. In the twentieth century Hidemaro Konoe arranged it for Western orchestra, and it is often the first gagaku that listeners hear.
image_caption: Koto and shō, two instruments of the gagaku ensemble, woodblock print, Library of Congress

title: Ranryō-ō
creator: imperial-household-gagaku
year: Tang origin; Japanese performance from 8th century
location: Imperial court and great shrines and temples
note: The most famous bugaku dance, a solo in a fierce dragon mask about a handsome prince who hid his face in battle.
description: Ranryō-ō, the 'King of Lanling', is based on the story of Gao Changgong, a prince of the Northern Qi in sixth-century China, so handsome that he wore a terrifying mask to frighten his enemies. A dance about him existed at the Tang court and came to Japan, traditionally in the Nara period. In bugaku a single dancer in a gilded dragon-topped mask with a movable jaw, orange robes and a baton performs vigorous yet stately movements to music of the Left, the Chinese-derived repertory. Old masks survive at Tōdai-ji, Itsukushima and elsewhere. It is performed at court, at Shitennō-ji's Shōryō-e and at Kasuga Wakamiya, and remains one of the best loved pieces of the repertory.
image_caption: Bugaku mask for Ryōō (Ranryō-ō), Masumida Shrine

title: Seigaiha
creator: imperial-household-gagaku
note: An elegant bugaku dance for two, made famous by the scene in The Tale of Genji where Genji dances it.
description: Seigaiha, 'blue ocean waves', is a dance of the Left for two dancers in costumes embroidered with waves and plovers, its music traditionally said to be of Indian origin. In the seventh chapter of The Tale of Genji, Hikaru Genji and his friend Tō no Chūjō dance it before the emperor beneath autumn leaves, and Genji's beauty moves the audience to tears. The overlapping wave pattern on the costumes gave its name to a design used across Japanese art. The dance is rarely performed today because of its demanding staging, but it remains a symbol of Heian courtly elegance.

title: Heikyoku: chanting The Tale of the Heike
creator: heike-storytellers
note: The chanting of the war tale to the biwa by blind monks, the foundation of Japanese narrative singing.
description: The Tale of the Heike was meant to be heard. Blind biwa hōshi chanted its episodes, the rise and fall of the Taira, the deaths of young warriors, the drowning of the child emperor, in a style that alternates almost spoken lines with melodic formulas and short lute interludes, each formula with its own name and expressive purpose. The text that the master Kakuichi dictated in 1371 became the standard. The art was organised in the blind guild, the Tōdōza, and in the Edo period was taught to samurai as a refined pastime. Its formulas and vocal style shaped Noh chant and the later jōruri of the puppet theatre. Today only a handful of performers carry on traditional heikyoku, though many modern biwa players draw on it. The tale itself is in the literature section.
image_caption: A biwa hōshi from a medieval picture scroll of poetry contests between artisans (Shokunin uta-awase)

title: Takasago
creator: zeami
note: A Noh of the gods in which the spirits of twin pines celebrate long marriage and the age of poetry; still sung at Japanese weddings.
description: A priest travelling from Kyushu to the capital stops at Takasago Bay, where an old couple sweep beneath a pine. They explain that this pine and the one at Sumiyoshi across the bay are a married pair, though far apart, and that pines stand for the eternity of Japanese poetry. Revealed as the spirits of the pines, they invite him to Sumiyoshi, where the god of Sumiyoshi appears in the second half and dances a vigorous dance under the moon. Takasago is the model of the first category of Noh, plays of gods, which opened a full programme, and it shows Zeami's art of weaving classical poetry into the text. A passage from it, 'Takasago ya', was long chanted at weddings, and the image of the old couple is a common New Year's decoration.
image_file: Takasago 高砂 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Takasago, from the print series Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Sotoba Komachi
creator: kanami
note: Kan'ami's play about the poet Ono no Komachi as a destitute old woman, who outwits priests and is possessed by a rejected lover.
description: Priests from Mount Kōya find a ragged old woman sitting on a stupa, a sacred grave marker, and rebuke her, but she argues with them so brilliantly about Buddhist doctrine that they bow to her. She is revealed as Ono no Komachi, once the most beautiful poet of the Heian court, now a hundred years old. Suddenly she is possessed by the spirit of Fukakusa no Shōshō, the suitor who died on the hundredth of the hundred nights he was told to visit her, and she acts out his journeys. The play, by Kan'ami and revised by Zeami, combines debate, madness and possession with a reflection on age and enlightenment. Mishima Yukio wrote a famous modern version in his Modern Noh Plays.
image_file: Sotoba Komachi 卒都婆小町 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Sotoba Komachi, from Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Matsukaze
creator: kanami
note: A dream Noh of two salt-making sisters whose love for the exiled poet Yukihira survives their death; often called the finest of all Noh.
description: At Suma Bay a monk sees a pine that marks the grave of two sisters, Matsukaze and Murasame, who loved the courtier poet Ariwara no Yukihira during his exile there. That night two women carrying salt-water pails come to the hut where he shelters; they are the sisters' ghosts. Matsukaze, overcome by memory, puts on Yukihira's hat and robe and dances, mistaking the pine for her lover, before the ghosts vanish at dawn, leaving only the wind in the pines. Zeami records that the play derives from Kan'ami's version of an older work, and that he himself revised it. With its moonlight, salt water and the motif of the pail reflecting the moon, it was rated by Zeami among the best plays and is one of the most admired works of the repertory.
image_file: Matsukaze 松風 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Matsukaze, from Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Hagoromo
creator: noh-playwrights
note: A celestial maiden must dance to recover her feather robe from a fisherman: the most popular Noh play.
description: On the pine beach at Miho, with Mount Fuji behind, the fisherman Hakuryō finds a beautiful feather robe hanging on a pine. A heavenly being (tennin) appears and begs for it, since without it she cannot return to the sky. He agrees to give it back if she will dance for him, and when he worries that she will fly away first, she replies that deceit is for humans, not heaven. She dances the dance of the moon palace, then rises over Fuji into the haze. Based on a widespread swan-maiden legend, the play has no tragic element and is loved for its lyricism and its long dance. Its author is unknown; old attributions to Zeami are not accepted.
image_file: Hagoromo 羽衣 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Hagoromo, from Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Dōjōji
creator: noh-playwrights
note: The great demon play of Noh, in which a woman's jealous spirit returns to the temple bell under which her lover hid.
description: At the Dōjōji temple in Kii province a new bell is being dedicated, and women are forbidden. A dancer arrives and persuades a servant to let her in, then performs a famous slow 'step-dance' (ranbyōshi) with the small drum, in which a single step can take minutes, before leaping up under the stage bell, which falls on her. The abbot tells the legend of a girl whose love for a travelling monk turned her into a serpent who coiled round the bell where he hid and burned him to death. When the bell is raised a serpent demon emerges and is driven off by the monks' prayers. The play, a reworking of the older Kanemaki, is one of the most demanding in the repertory, and the legend was adapted in the kabuki dance Musume Dōjōji.
image_file: Dōjōji 道成寺 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Dōjōji, from Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Okina
creator: noh-playwrights
note: A ritual blessing of the land performed by actors in masks of smiling old men, older than Noh drama itself.
description: Okina is said to be 'Noh and yet not Noh'. It has no plot. The actors purify themselves before the performance, and in the dance the main actor puts on the white Okina mask on stage, before the audience, to become a god who blesses the realm with peace and abundance; the black-masked Sanbasō, danced by a kyōgen actor, follows with a vigorous rice-planting dance shaking a bell tree. It derives from ritual sarugaku performances at temples and shrines that existed before Kan'ami and Zeami, and it was performed at the start of a formal programme and at New Year. Its masks are among the oldest objects of Noh, and Sanbasō dances passed into kabuki and bunraku.
image_file: Okina 翁 - Nōgaku hyakuban 能樂百番 - Tsukioka Kōgyo 月岡耕漁 (Art Institute of Chicago).jpg
image_caption: Tsukioka Kōgyo, Okina, from Nōgaku hyakuban, Art Institute of Chicago

title: Busu
creator: kyogen-actors
note: A kyōgen farce in which two servants eat their master's 'poison', which is really sugar.
description: A master goes out, telling his servants Tarōkaja and Jirōkaja to watch a lacquered tub that contains busu, a deadly poison that kills even if the wind blows from it. Curious, they fan the air away and look inside, and find it is sugar, which they eat to the last grain. To explain themselves they tear a precious scroll and smash a valuable bowl, and when the master returns they weep that, having broken his treasures, they tried to kill themselves with poison but could not die. The story has parallels in Chinese and Japanese folk tales and in Buddhist collections. It is one of the most frequently played kyōgen and is read in Japanese school textbooks.

title: Bōshibari
creator: kyogen-actors
note: A kyōgen in which a master ties his servants up to keep them from his sake, and they drink it anyway.
description: Tired of his servants raiding the sake while he is out, a master ties Jirōkaja's arms to his back and Tarōkaja's to a pole across his shoulders. The two bound servants manage to open the storehouse and feed each other sake from the lid of the cask, then sing and dance in their bonds. The master returns to find them drunk, and they mock him, seeing his face reflected in the sake. The play shows the physical comedy and the sympathy for the servant that are typical of kyōgen, and it is among the best known in the West.

title: Okuni kabuki
creator: izumo-no-okuni
location: Bed of the Kamo River, Kyoto
note: Okuni's dances and sketches in Kyoto in 1603, the first kabuki performances.
description: In the spring of 1603, the year Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun, Okuni and her troupe performed on a temporary stage on the riverbed of the Kamo in Kyoto. Her programme combined Buddhist nenbutsu dance with a scandalous sketch in which she, dressed as a fashionable young man with a sword and a Christian rosary, visited a teahouse girl played by a man. The novelty, a mixture of dance, song and erotic comedy, was immediately copied, and painted screens and illustrated scrolls of the early seventeenth century depict these performances. The women's kabuki that followed was suppressed in 1629, but the name and many elements of Okuni's art passed into the all-male kabuki of the Edo period.
image_file: Okuni kabuki byobu-zu cropped and enhanced.jpg
image_caption: Detail of an early 17th-century folding screen showing Okuni kabuki

title: Shibaraku
creator: ichikawa-danjuro-i
note: The archetypal aragoto scene: a superhero cries 'Wait a moment!' and saves the innocent from a tyrant.
description: Shibaraku, 'Just a moment!', began as a scene that Danjūrō I inserted into the annual opening (kaomise) plays of Edo theatres from 1697. Just as a villainous lord is about to execute innocent people, a voice cries out from the back of the theatre and the hero enters along the hanamichi walkway in vast persimmon-coloured robes with the family crest, red-and-white kumadori make-up, a huge sword and a fan-like headdress, to rescue them with superhuman strength. The scene, repeated with variations for over a century, became one of the Kabuki Jūhachiban, the eighteen great plays of the Ichikawa family, and its costume and poses are among the most familiar images of kabuki.
image_caption: Utagawa Kuniyoshi, woodblock print of an actor in Shibaraku

title: Sukeroku
creator: ichikawa-danjuro-ii
note: Danjūrō II's play about a dashing dandy of the Yoshiwara pleasure quarter, in reality a samurai seeking a stolen sword.
description: First staged in 1713 and refined over the following decades, Sukeroku presents Hanakawado Sukeroku, the picture of Edo style in a black kimono, purple headband and yellow socks, who picks quarrels in the Yoshiwara in order to make men draw their swords. He is really the warrior Soga no Gorō, searching for a sword stolen from his family, and his rival the arrogant samurai Ikyū has it. His lover is the great courtesan Agemaki. The play is famous for its spectacular entrance along the hanamichi, accompanied by the singing of a special style of jōruri called katōbushi, and for its portrait of Edo city culture. It is one of the Kabuki Jūhachiban.
image_file: Sukeroku, from the series The Eighteen Great Kabuki Plays.jpg
image_caption: Sukeroku, from the print series The Eighteen Great Kabuki Plays

title: Kanjinchō
creator: ichikawa-danjuro-vii
note: The kabuki adaptation of the Noh play Ataka, in which the loyal Benkei bluffs their way past a barrier to save Yoshitsune.
description: Fleeing his brother the shogun, the warrior Yoshitsune and his retainers, disguised as mountain priests, are stopped at the Ataka barrier. To prove they are collecting funds for Tōdai-ji, Benkei reads aloud an empty scroll as if it were a subscription list (kanjinchō). When the guards recognise Yoshitsune, Benkei beats his master to prove he is only a porter, and the barrier keeper Togashi, moved, lets them through. Danjūrō VII adapted the play from Noh in 1840, with a stage set imitating the Noh pine and nagauta music by Kineya Rokusaburō IV. Its climax, Benkei's 'flying six directions' exit along the hanamichi, is one of kabuki's most celebrated moments, and it became the most frequently performed of the Kabuki Jūhachiban.
image_file: Ebizō Ichikawa V as Benkei and Danjūrō Ichikawa VIII as Tokashi.jpg
image_caption: Woodblock print of Ichikawa Ebizō V (Danjūrō VII) as Benkei and Danjūrō VIII as Togashi

title: Shusse Kagekiyo
creator: chikamatsu-monzaemon
note: The first play Chikamatsu wrote for Takemoto Gidayū, traditionally taken as the start of 'new jōruri'.
description: Kagekiyo Victorious tells of the Taira warrior Kagekiyo, who plans to assassinate the victorious Minamoto Yoritomo, is betrayed by his jealous mistress, escapes and is captured, and finally blinds himself so that he will never again see his enemy. Written by Chikamatsu for Gidayū's new theatre in 1685, it gave the hero a more human psychology and introduced elements of Noh drama, and later critics regarded it as dividing old jōruri from new. It began the partnership between playwright and chanter that dominated the Osaka puppet stage for two decades.

title: Gidayū-bushi and the Takemoto-za
creator: takemoto-gidayu
note: The style of narrative chanting with shamisen founded by Gidayū in 1684, still the voice of bunraku.
description: When Takemoto Gidayū opened his puppet theatre in Osaka in 1684, he brought a powerful new manner of narration that fused earlier jōruri styles with Noh chant and popular song. The tayū sits at the side of the stage with a text on a lacquered stand, speaking and singing every character as well as the narration, while a shamisen player beside him supports and goads him. The style soon dominated puppet theatre and passed to kabuki, where gidayū musicians accompany plays adapted from bunraku. It was also performed in concert, and from the Meiji period young women sang it in a craze called musume gidayū. In modern bunraku the tayū, shamisen and three-man puppets are equally esteemed, and the art was proclaimed UNESCO Intangible Heritage in 2003 (listed 2008).
image_file: Ōmi no kuni Shiga monogatari - Takemoto Gidayū - btv1b10878888q (01 of 19).jpg
image_caption: Printed chanting text of the Takemoto school, Bibliothèque nationale de France

title: Kanadehon Chūshingura
creator: takeda-izumo-ii
note: The story of the forty-seven loyal retainers in eleven acts, the most popular play of Japanese theatre.
description: In 1701 a daimyō drew his sword in the shogun's castle against an official who had insulted him and was ordered to commit suicide; in 1703 forty-seven of his former retainers killed the official and then gave themselves up and died by seppuku. Censorship barred direct portrayal of recent events, so the playwrights Takeda Izumo II, Namiki Senryū I and Miyoshi Shōraku moved the story to the fourteenth century and gave the characters medieval names. The play, first performed by puppets in 1748 and staged by kabuki the same year, follows the leader Ōboshi Yuranosuke as he hides his revenge behind a life of dissipation, while ordinary people suffer for their loyalty. In the Edo period it was said that a theatre in difficulty need only stage Chūshingura to recover. It inspired countless prints, novels and films and remains the single best-known story of loyalty in Japan.
image_caption: Utagawa Kuniteru, Act III of Kanadehon Chūshingura, woodblock print

title: Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura
creator: takeda-izumo-ii
note: Yoshitsune and the Thousand Cherry Trees: a play of the defeated Taira in disguise, and a fox who loves a drum.
description: In this five-act play the fugitive hero Yoshitsune is surrounded by stories of others. The Taira generals reported dead at Dan-no-ura are in fact alive and in hiding, one as a boatman, another as a sushi shop apprentice, and they face their fate in some of the most famous scenes of the repertory. A fox, disguised as Yoshitsune's retainer Tadanobu, follows his lady because the drum she carries is made from the skin of its parents. Written by Takeda Izumo II, Namiki Senryū I and Miyoshi Shōraku, it was first performed by puppets in 1747 and is a cornerstone of both bunraku and kabuki, where the acrobatic fox scenes are a showpiece.
image_caption: Utagawa Kuniyoshi, print of Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura, 1848

title: Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami
creator: takeda-izumo-ii
note: Sugawara and the Secrets of Calligraphy: the exile of the minister Michizane, with the famous scene 'The Village School'.
description: The play takes the historical exile of the Heian minister Sugawara no Michizane, later worshipped as the god of learning, and builds around it the story of triplet brothers serving different masters. In its most famous act, 'Terakoya' (The Village School), a schoolmaster must deliver the head of Michizane's young son to his enemies, and the retainer Matsuōmaru, sent to identify the head, has secretly sacrificed his own son as a substitute. The play premiered with puppets in 1746 and was soon adapted for kabuki. Its scenes of agonised duty made it, with Chūshingura and Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura, one of the three great masterpieces of the puppet theatre.
image_file: Nakazō Nakamura II as Matsuō-maru and as Noshio Nakamura II Chiyo.jpg
image_caption: Woodblock print of Nakamura Nakazō II as Matsuōmaru and Nakamura Noshio II as Chiyo

title: Rokudan no Shirabe
creator: yatsuhashi-kengyo
note: The most famous koto piece, six variations of 52 beats each, traditionally attributed to Yatsuhashi Kengyō.
description: Rokudan, 'six sections', is a purely instrumental piece in the danmono form: six sections of equal length, each of fifty-two beats (except the first), beginning slowly and accelerating, with each section a free variation on a common framework. It is played on the thirteen-string koto in the hira-jōshi tuning, and its spare, rising opening phrase is known to almost every Japanese. The attribution to Yatsuhashi rests on tradition, and its early sources are from the eighteenth century. It became the first piece learned by koto students and is often played as a duet with shakuhachi or shamisen. Some scholars have proposed a link with Christian chant heard in sixteenth-century Japan, an idea that remains speculative.
image_file: Beauty Playing the Koto Zither-by Suzuki Harunobu-Tokyo National Museum.jpg
image_caption: Suzuki Harunobu, Beauty Playing the Koto, Tokyo National Museum

title: Midare
creator: yatsuhashi-kengyo
note: A koto danmono with irregular sections and changing tempos, prized for its freedom.
description: Midare, 'disorder', also called Midare rinzetsu, is a danmono like Rokudan but with sections of unequal length and frequent tempo changes, so that it seems to unfold freely. It is attributed to Yatsuhashi, though the version played today was probably reworked by later players. It is among the most admired works of the classical koto repertory and a test of a player's sense of timing and tone.
image_file: A koto or Japanese zither LCCN2009630122.jpg
image_caption: A koto, woodblock print, Library of Congress

title: Tsuru no Sugomori
creator: kurosawa-kinko
note: 'Nesting of the Cranes', a shakuhachi honkyoku that imitates the life of cranes with fluttering tones.
description: Tsuru no Sugomori is one of the most famous pieces of shakuhachi music, existing in versions in the Kinko, Tozan and regional traditions. It portrays the life of a crane family, from the building of the nest to the raising of the chicks and their flight, using the 'koro-koro' flutter-tonguing and rolling techniques that imitate the cries and wingbeats of cranes. Its origins are unknown and it may have existed before the Kinko-ryū, which transmits a version among its secondary pieces. Because of its descriptive character it is unusual among honkyoku, which are usually meditative, and it is often played at celebrations, the crane being a symbol of long life.
image_caption: A komusō playing the shakuhachi, woodblock print, Library of Congress

title: Shika no Tōne
creator: kurosawa-kinko
note: 'The Distant Cry of the Deer', a duet for two shakuhachi in which two deer call to each other across autumn hills.
description: Shika no Tōne is one of the core honkyoku of the Kinko-ryū, arranged in the collection that Kurosawa Kinko assembled from the pieces played at Fuke temples. Two players, often standing apart, answer each other in long, sliding phrases, which gradually overlap and come together, evoking the mating call of deer in the autumn mountains, a classical image of loneliness in Japanese poetry. It is one of the most frequently performed shakuhachi works and shows how the honkyoku combine breath, tone colour and silence.
image_file: 風俗六玉川-A Young Komuso MET DP144638.jpg
image_caption: A young komusō, woodblock print, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Chidori no Kyoku
creator: yoshizawa-kengyo
note: 'Song of the Plovers', a koto and kokyū song on classical poems with a famous interlude imitating plovers.
description: Chidori no Kyoku sets two poems about plovers, small shore birds, one from the Kokinshū and one from the Kin'yōshū, in Yoshizawa's archaic kokin-gumi style, framed by a long instrumental interlude whose rippling figures suggest waves and the cries of birds over the beach at Awaji. Yoshizawa wrote it for koto with the kokyū fiddle, though it is now often played with shakuhachi. Its clear, restrained manner, consciously reaching back to court music, made it one of the most popular koto works and a model for Meiji composers.

title: Kōjō no Tsuki
creator: rentaro-taki
note: 'The Moon over the Ruined Castle', Taki's elegiac school song, among the best-known Japanese songs.
description: Commissioned for a songbook for middle schools, Kōjō no Tsuki sets a poem by Doi Bansui contrasting the moonlit cherry-blossom banquets of a castle in its days of glory with its ruins and the unchanging moon. Taki's melody, in a minor-like mode that sounds both Japanese and Western, is said to be inspired by the ruined Oka Castle at Taketa, where he spent part of his boyhood. It was originally published unaccompanied; Yamada Kōsaku later made a piano arrangement, changing a note and slowing it, and this version is often sung today. The song has been recorded by singers, choirs and jazz musicians, including Thelonious Monk.

title: Hana
creator: rentaro-taki
location: Part of the cycle Shiki (Four Seasons), Tokyo
note: 'Flowers', Taki's spring song for two voices about cherry blossoms on the Sumida River.
description: Hana is the first song of Taki's four-part cycle Shiki (The Four Seasons), published in 1900, and sets a poem by Takeshima Hagoromo about boats rowing on the Sumida River among cherry blossoms. Written as a duet with piano, it is one of the earliest Japanese art songs and remains a standard for school and amateur choirs, sung each spring.

title: Akatombo
creator: kosaku-yamada
note: 'Red Dragonfly', Yamada's setting of Miki Rofū's nostalgic poem, one of Japan's best-loved songs.
description: Miki Rofū's poem remembers seeing red dragonflies at sunset as a child, carried on the back of a young nursemaid who later married and left. Yamada's 1927 setting follows the pitch accents of the Japanese words closely in a gentle pentatonic melody. Recorded and sung in schools, it became one of the most familiar songs in Japan, often played at dusk by public loudspeakers. The work is still in copyright.

title: Haru no Umi
creator: michio-miyagi
note: 'The Sea in Spring', Miyagi's duet for koto and shakuhachi, the most famous modern piece of Japanese traditional music.
description: Miyagi wrote Haru no Umi for the Imperial poetry reading of 1930, whose theme was 'The Sea near Rocks', inspired by memories of the Inland Sea at Tomonoura. In three parts, it pairs the koto with the shakuhachi in a lively, transparent dialogue suggesting waves, birds and the songs of fishermen, using Western-influenced form and harmony. After Miyagi recorded it with the French violinist Renée Chemet in 1932, playing violin in place of shakuhachi, it became internationally known. It is played at Japanese New Year and is one of the most recorded works for traditional instruments. The work is still in copyright.

title: November Steps
creator: takemitsu
type: Concerto for biwa, shakuhachi and orchestra
location: Lincoln Center, New York (New York Philharmonic, Seiji Ozawa)
note: Takemitsu's double concerto pitting the biwa and shakuhachi against the orchestra, a landmark of East–West music.
description: Commissioned for the 125th anniversary of the New York Philharmonic and premiered in November 1967 under Seiji Ozawa, November Steps features Tsuruta Kinshi on satsuma biwa and Yokoyama Katsuya on shakuhachi. Takemitsu did not try to blend the two worlds: the orchestra, divided into two mirrored groups, frames long passages in which the traditional instruments play alone, with their noises, breath and silence. The title refers to the eleven 'steps' or sections, playing on the Japanese term dan. The work made Takemitsu internationally famous and helped launch a wider interest in Japanese instruments among composers. It is still in copyright.

title: The gayageum and Ureuk's twelve pieces
creator: ureuk
note: The twelve-string zither of Gaya, for which Ureuk wrote twelve pieces; it became the national instrument of Korea.
description: The Samguk sagi records that King Gasil of Gaya, wishing his kingdom to have its own music, had a zither made and commanded Ureuk to compose twelve pieces named after the districts of Gaya. Ureuk brought the instrument to Silla, where it became part of court music, and a Silla zither of the eighth century, the shiragi-goto, survives in the Shōsōin at Nara. The gayageum has twelve silk strings stretched over movable bridges on a long hollow body, plucked with the fingers of the right hand while the left hand presses the strings to bend and vibrate the pitches, giving Korean music its characteristic expressive ornaments. The twelve pieces are lost, but the instrument has been played continuously for fifteen centuries, in court music (pungnyu gayageum) and folk music (sanjo gayageum), and modern versions have up to twenty-five strings.
image_caption: A pungnyu (court-style) gayageum

title: Pyeonggyeong of 1427 (Korean stone chimes)
creator: bak-yeon
location: Joseon court, Hanseong; tradition continued at the National Gugak Center, Seoul
note: The set of sixteen L-shaped stone chimes made by Bak Yeon from Korean stone, foundation of Joseon ritual music.
description: Stone chimes, with bells the fixed-pitch instruments of Confucian ritual orchestras, had to be imported from China, and the set used in Korea was incomplete and poorly tuned. In 1425 a suitable stone was found at Namyang, and Bak Yeon used it to make a new set of sixteen chimes in two rows, hung in a decorated frame and tuned to twelve pipes he had reconstructed from ancient texts. When the set was tested before King Sejong in 1433, the king is recorded as noticing that one chime was slightly high, and on inspection a line of ink was found on the stone where the mason had not finished grinding it, a story often told of Sejong's ear. The pyeonggyeong and the matching bronze bells (pyeonjong) are still central to the aak of the Munmyo and Jongmyo shrines.
image_caption: A Joseon pyeonggyeong, National Palace Museum of Korea

title: Jongmyo jeryeak
creator: sejong
note: The music and dance of the Joseon royal ancestral rites, performed every year at Jongmyo for over five centuries.
description: The rites at Jongmyo, the shrine of the Joseon kings and queens in Seoul, are accompanied by music and the line dance ilmu. The music consists of two suites, Botaepyeong (Preserving the Peace) praising the civil virtues of the dynastic founders, and Jeongdaeeop (Establishing the Great Enterprise) praising their military achievements. King Sejong composed them in the 1440s for banquets, drawing on Korean and Chinese-derived styles, and his son Sejo adopted them for the ancestral rites in 1464. Two ensembles, one on the upper terrace and one below, play bells, stone chimes, drums, oboes, flutes and zithers while a choir sings Chinese texts. The rites were interrupted in the early twentieth century and restored in 1969, and since 1971 they have been held annually in May by the Jeonju Yi clan with the National Gugak Center. In 2001 the Jongmyo rite and its music were proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO.
image_file: Korean Royal Ancestral Ritual Music-Jongmyo Jeryeak-01.jpg
image_caption: Performance of the Jongmyo ritual music at the shrine

title: Yeominlak
creator: sejong
note: 'Enjoying Peace with the People', Sejong's setting of the Songs of the Dragons Flying to Heaven, still played as slow court music.
description: Yeominlak was composed under Sejong to sing the Yongbieocheonga (Songs of the Dragons Flying to Heaven), the first long text written in the new Korean alphabet, which praised the founders of the Joseon dynasty. Its notation in jeongganbo appears in the Sejong sillok. The version played today is purely instrumental and very slow, in several forms for different ensembles, and is one of the representative pieces of Korean court music, with its stately rhythm, the wide vibrato of the oboe piri and the sound of the large bamboo flute daegeum.

title: Jeongganbo notation
creator: sejong
location: Joseon court; scores in the Sejong sillok
note: The first East Asian notation to show exact rhythm, a grid of squares devised at Sejong's court.
description: Chinese and Korean music had long been notated with pitch names, but without a precise way to write duration. Jeongganbo, 'well-square notation', solved this by writing music in columns of squares, each square (jeonggan) representing one unit of time, so that the number of squares a note occupies shows its length. The pitch is written inside the square in Chinese pitch-names or abbreviated syllables, and later forms added ornaments and the rhythm of the hourglass drum. The system is first found in the music scores of the Annals of King Sejong and is traditionally credited to the king himself. It remained in use throughout the Joseon dynasty and is still used to write Korean traditional music today.
image_caption: Siyong hyangakbo, a 16th-century score book written in jeongganbo

title: Sujecheon
creator: korean-court-musicians
year: origin c. 7th century (traditional); present form Joseon
location: Korean court; National Gugak Center, Seoul
note: 'Longevity as Eternal as the Heavens', the oldest surviving piece of Korean court music, of majestic slowness.
description: Sujecheon is believed to derive from a song of the Baekje kingdom, Jeongeupsa, about a woman who climbs a hill to await her husband's return, though this tradition is uncertain. Transmitted as instrumental court music, it was played for royal banquets and processions, and it is often described as the oldest music in the Korean repertory still performed. It is played by a wind-dominated ensemble led by the piri oboe, with daegeum flute, haegeum fiddle, ajaeng and drums, in a free, extremely slow rhythm in which each phrase swells and fades. Its grandeur has made it a symbol of the Korean court tradition, and it is often played at state occasions.

title: Akhak gwebeom
creator: korean-court-musicians
location: Compiled at the Joseon court by Seong Hyeon and others
note: 'Guide to the Study of Music', the great Joseon encyclopedia of court music, instruments, dance and costume.
description: Commissioned by King Seongjong and completed in 1493 by Seong Hyeon and other officials, the Akhak gwebeom describes the theory, instruments, performances, dances, costumes and stage properties of the court's ritual aak, Chinese-derived dangak and native hyangak. Its illustrations of every instrument with measurements made it the reference for reconstructing instruments after the Japanese invasions of the 1590s destroyed many, and it is still used by makers today. It also records the words of Goryeo songs that would otherwise be lost. It is one of the most important sources for the history of Korean music.
image_caption: A copy of the Akhak gwebeom

title: Chunhyangga
creator: pansori-singers
note: The most popular pansori, the love story of Chunhyang and Yi Mong-ryong, which can take eight hours to perform in full.
description: Chunhyangga tells of Chunhyang, daughter of a courtesan in Namwon, who secretly marries Yi Mong-ryong, the son of the local magistrate. When he leaves for the capital, the new magistrate demands her favours, and she is beaten and imprisoned for refusing. Mong-ryong returns as a secret royal inspector, at first disguised as a beggar, and saves her. The singer, standing with a fan, plays all the roles and alternates song (sori), narrative speech (aniri) and gesture (ballim), while a drummer on the buk sets the rhythmic cycles and calls out encouragement (chuimsae). Famous passages include the love song (Sarangga) and the scene of Chunhyang's beating (Sipjangga). It is the longest and most varied of the five surviving pansori and exists in versions of several lineages. The story itself is discussed in the literature section.

title: Simcheongga
creator: pansori-singers
note: The pansori of Sim Cheong, who sells herself as a sacrifice to the sea so her blind father may regain his sight.
description: Sim Cheong, raised by her blind father, hears that a temple offering of three hundred sacks of rice will restore his sight, and sells herself to sailors who need a maiden to sacrifice to the sea god. Thrown into the waves, she is saved by the Dragon King, returns in a lotus flower and becomes queen, and holds a banquet for all the blind men of the land, where her father regains his sight at the sound of her voice. Simcheongga is renowned for its tragic passages, sung in the sorrowful gyemyeonjo mode, and is often regarded as the most moving of the pansori. Isang Yun's opera Sim Tjong (1972) is based on the story.

title: Sugungga
creator: pansori-singers
note: The comic pansori of the Underwater Palace, in which a turtle tries to bring a rabbit's liver to cure the Dragon King.
description: The Dragon King of the Southern Sea falls ill, and only the liver of a rabbit can cure him. A turtle is sent to the land, flatters a rabbit with tales of the palace and brings it under the sea, where the rabbit, realising the danger, claims to have left its liver on land to dry and escapes. A satire of officials and courtiers, rooted in an old Buddhist fable, it is the most comic and allegorical of the five surviving pansori.

title: Heungboga
creator: pansori-singers
note: The pansori of two brothers, the kind poor Heungbo and the greedy rich Nolbo, and the gourd seeds a swallow brings.
description: Heungbo, cast out by his greedy elder brother Nolbo, mends the broken leg of a swallow, which brings him a gourd seed; the gourds that grow from it are full of treasure. Nolbo breaks a swallow's leg to win the same fortune, but his gourds release goblins and disasters. The pansori is full of humour, especially in the scene of sawing open the gourds, and its tale of kindness rewarded is known to every Korean.

title: Jeokbyeokga
creator: pansori-singers
note: The pansori of the Battle of the Red Cliffs, the only one to take its story from Chinese history.
description: Jeokbyeokga retells the Battle of the Red Cliffs of 208, from the Chinese Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which Cao Cao's fleet is burned by the allied forces of Liu Bei and Sun Quan, and Cao Cao flees in humiliation. Korean singers added scenes of the suffering of common soldiers and a satirical portrait of Cao Cao. It requires a powerful, masculine voice and was long the favourite of male master singers.

title: Gwangdaega (Song of the Singer)
creator: shin-jae-hyo
note: Shin Jae-hyo's song on the art of pansori, naming the four essentials of a singer.
description: In Gwangdaega Shin Jae-hyo set out in verse what a pansori singer needs: first, presence (inmul); second, the text (sasol); third, a well-trained voice (deugeum); and fourth, acting and gesture (neoreumsae). He compared the master singers of his day to great Chinese poets. The song is the first piece of pansori criticism and, with his edited texts of six pansori, shows how the genre was becoming a recognised art for educated audiences in the late nineteenth century.

title: Gayageum sanjo
creator: kim-chang-jo
note: The virtuoso solo suite for gayageum and drum, moving from slow to fast rhythmic cycles, created by Kim Chang-jo.
description: Sanjo, 'scattered melodies', is a suite of movements for a solo instrument and the janggu drum, each in a different rhythmic cycle (jangdan): the slow jinyangjo, then jungmori, jungjungmori, jajinmori and the fast hwimori and danmori, so that the music accelerates over thirty minutes to an hour. It draws on the modes and melodies of pansori and shamanic sinawi and gives the performer room for personal expression and improvisation. Kim Chang-jo is credited with creating the first gayageum sanjo in the late nineteenth century, and his pupils' versions, such as those of the Kim Juk-pa and Seong Geum-yeon schools, are still taught. Sanjo for geomungo, daegeum, haegeum, ajaeng and piri followed, and it became the central genre of solo instrumental music in Korea.

title: Arirang
creator: korean-folk-singers
note: Korea's best-known folk song, existing in thousands of regional versions, with its refrain of crossing the Arirang pass.
description: Arirang is not a single song but a family of folk songs sharing the refrain 'Arirang, arirang, arariyo' and the image of crossing the Arirang pass. Regional forms such as Jeongseon Arirang, Jindo Arirang and Miryang Arirang have very different melodies and texts. The standard 'Bonjo Arirang' became known nationwide after it was used in Na Un-gyu's silent film Arirang (1926), a story of resistance under Japanese rule. The song became a symbol of longing, separation and national identity, sung by Koreans in the North and the South and abroad, and the combined Korean team marched to it at the Olympics. It was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list by South Korea in 2012 and by North Korea in 2014.

title: Réak
creator: isang-yun
note: Isang Yun's orchestral breakthrough, a Western modernist work modelled on the sound of Korean court music.
description: Réak takes its title from the Korean word for ritual music (yeak), and was written for the Donaueschingen Festival of 1966. Its sustained tones, swelling and decaying with glissandi and vibrato, and its punctuating clapper strokes evoke the opening of Korean court and ritual music, while the language is entirely that of the European avant-garde. It established Yun's international reputation shortly before his abduction from West Berlin in 1967. It is still in copyright.

title: Chimhyangmu
creator: hwang-byungki
note: 'Dance in the Fragrance of Aloes', Hwang Byungki's best-known gayageum piece, inspired by Silla Buddhist art.
description: Chimhyangmu was inspired by Buddhist art of the Silla period and the imagined dances of the heavenly beings depicted on it. Hwang used a special tuning and the full resources of the gayageum, with the janggu drum, to create a piece that moves from meditative opening to rhythmic dance. It became one of the most frequently performed works for gayageum, a model for later Korean composers writing for traditional instruments. It is still in copyright.

title: Korea Fantasy
creator: ahn-eak-tai
note: Ahn Eak-tai's symphonic poem on Korean history, ending with the melody adopted as South Korea's national anthem.
description: The Korea Fantasy is a symphonic poem in several sections depicting Korean history from its foundation through the suffering of the Japanese occupation to liberation, closing with a choral setting of the Aegukga (Patriotic Song). Ahn had written that melody in 1935 to replace the Scottish tune 'Auld Lang Syne' to which the text had been sung. It was adopted by the provisional government in exile and later by the Republic of Korea. The work was revised several times, adding a section on the Korean War. Controversy over Ahn's wartime career has led to debates about the anthem. It is still in copyright.

title: Ambush from Ten Sides (Shimian maifu)
creator: chinese-folk-musicians
location: Printed in Hua Qiuping's Pipa pu (Wuxi, 1818)
note: A martial pipa suite depicting the battle of Gaixia (202 BC), with its famous sounds of clashing armies.
description: Ambush from Ten Sides depicts the final battle between Liu Bang, founder of the Han, and Xiang Yu, King of Chu, at Gaixia in 202 BC, in which Xiang Yu's army was surrounded and destroyed. In a series of titled sections, the pipa represents the camps, the sounding of the drums and horns, the battle, the noise of horses and swords and Xiang Yu's death at the Wu River, using strummed chords, string-pulling, slaps and buzzes. The piece belongs to the 'martial' (wu) style of pipa music and was first printed in the collection of Hua Qiuping in 1818, though its legend claims older roots. Its companion is the 'civil' piece The Tyrant Removes His Armour. It is one of the most famous showpieces of Chinese instrumental music.
image_caption: A Chinese pipa, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Jasmine Flower (Mo li hua)
creator: chinese-folk-musicians
location: Jiangsu folk song; published in John Barrow, Travels in China (London, 1804)
note: China's most famous folk song outside China, transcribed by a British diplomat and quoted by Puccini in Turandot.
description: Mo li hua, praising the jasmine flower, exists in many regional versions, of which the Jiangsu version is the best known. It was heard by members of Lord Macartney's embassy to the Qianlong emperor in 1793, and a transcription appeared in John Barrow's Travels in China in 1804, one of the first Chinese melodies published in Europe. Puccini used it as a recurring theme in Turandot (1926). In China it has been sung at state ceremonies and was performed at the Hong Kong handover and the Beijing Olympics.

title: Spring River Flower Moon Night (Chunjiang huayue ye)
creator: chinese-folk-musicians
note: An arrangement for Chinese ensemble of the old pipa piece Flute and Drum at Sunset, named after a Tang poem.
description: The pipa piece Xiyang xiao gu (Flute and Drum at Sunset) was printed in the nineteenth century and evokes a river at evening. In 1925 Liu Yaozhang and Zheng Jinwen of the Datong Music Society in Shanghai arranged it for an ensemble of Chinese instruments and named it after Zhang Ruoxu's famous Tang poem 'A Moonlit Night on the Spring River'. In ten sections, it became a classic of the new Chinese orchestra and is one of the best known pieces of Chinese instrumental music.

title: The Moon Reflected on the Second Spring (Erquan yingyue)
creator: abing
location: Recorded in Wuxi by Yang Yinliu and Cao Anhe (1950)
note: Abing's melancholy erhu solo, the best-known piece for the instrument.
description: Abing played this piece in the streets of Wuxi without a fixed title; when musicologists recorded it in 1950 he and they named it after the 'Second Spring under Heaven' at Wuxi's Huishan temple. It consists of a long melody repeated and varied six times with growing intensity, played in the lower register of the erhu with sliding ornaments that give it a sorrowful, introspective character. After Abing's death the recording was published and the piece was transcribed, taught at conservatories and arranged for Chinese and Western orchestras. Its moving quality, and the legend of the blind musician, made it the emblematic work of the erhu.
image_caption: An erhu, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: Dingjunshan
creator: tan-xinpei
note: The first Chinese film: scenes of the Three Kingdoms general Huang Zhong, played by Tan Xinpei.
description: Dingjunshan (Mount Dingjun) is a Peking opera about the aged general Huang Zhong, who defeats the Wei commander Xiahou Yuan in 219 and proves that age has not weakened him, a showpiece for laosheng singers. In 1905 Ren Qingtai of the Fengtai photo studio in Beijing filmed Tan Xinpei performing excerpts of the fighting scenes, the first film made in China. The short silent film was lost, possibly in a fire, but stills survive, and the event is celebrated as the birth of Chinese cinema.

title: Farewell My Concubine (Bawang bie ji)
creator: mei-lanfang
note: Mei Lanfang's tragedy of Xiang Yu and his consort Yu Ji, who dances with two swords before taking her own life.
description: Surrounded by the Han army at Gaixia and hearing the songs of Chu from the enemy camp, the defeated King of Chu, Xiang Yu, drinks with his beloved consort Yu Ji. She dances for him with two swords, then kills herself so that he can fight free. Mei Lanfang created the play in 1922 with the writer Qi Rushan and the actor Yang Xiaolou as Xiang Yu, based on older plays about the same events. Yu Ji's sword dance was one of his most famous creations. It became one of the most popular Peking operas and gave its name to Chen Kaige's film of 1993. It is still in copyright.

title: The Drunken Concubine (Guifei zuijiu)
creator: mei-lanfang
note: Yang Guifei, waiting in vain for the emperor, grows drunk in the Hundred Flowers Pavilion: Mei Lanfang's signature role.
description: The short opera shows Yang Guifei, who has prepared a banquet for Emperor Xuanzong only to learn that he has gone to another consort. Hurt, she drinks alone, sinking into intoxication in a famous series of dance movements, including backbends to drink from a cup on a tray. The play existed in the nineteenth century, and Mei Lanfang learned it from the actor Lu Sanbao, then refined it over decades, removing vulgar elements and stressing the heroine's loneliness. It became the signature work of the Mei school.

title: March of the Volunteers
creator: nie-er
location: Shanghai; theme of the film Children of Troubled Times
note: Nie Er's rousing song of resistance to Japan, adopted as the national anthem of the People's Republic of China.
description: Tian Han wrote the words and Nie Er the music for the film Children of Troubled Times, made in Shanghai in 1935 after Japan's seizure of Manchuria. Its call for people who refuse to be slaves to build a new Great Wall with their flesh and blood spread rapidly during the war, and in 1949 it was chosen as the provisional national anthem of the People's Republic; it was confirmed in the constitution in 1982 after a period in the Cultural Revolution when Tian Han was persecuted and the words were not sung. It is still in copyright in some countries through its lyricist.

title: Yellow River Cantata
creator: xian-xinghai
note: Xian Xinghai's eight-movement choral cantata on the Yellow River and the war against Japan.
description: The poet Guang Weiran wrote the text after crossing the Yellow River with a resistance troupe, and Xian Xinghai composed the music in a few days in Yan'an in March 1939, for the small forces available, including Chinese instruments. Its eight movements include the 'Song of the Yellow River Boatmen', an ode to the river, a lament and the climactic 'Defend the Yellow River', a round for mass singing, and 'Roar, Yellow River'. Revised by Xian in Moscow and later arranged for full orchestra, it became one of the defining works of modern Chinese music. In 1969 a group of composers led by Yin Chengzong reworked it as the Yellow River Piano Concerto, which became internationally famous.

title: The Butterfly Lovers Violin Concerto
creator: he-zhanhao
location: Shanghai Conservatory (premiere May 1959, soloist Yu Lina)
note: The most popular Chinese orchestral work, based on the legend of Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, written with Chen Gang.
description: The concerto tells the folk legend of Zhu Yingtai, who disguises herself as a man to study and falls in love with her classmate Liang Shanbo, who dies of grief when she is promised to another; at his grave she joins him in death, and the lovers turn into butterflies. He Zhanhao and Chen Gang wrote it as students at the Shanghai Conservatory for the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic, basing its themes on the melodies of Yue opera. The single-movement work uses Romantic Western forms while the violin imitates the slides and ornaments of Chinese fiddles and singers. It is the most recorded Chinese orchestral piece. It is still in copyright.

title: Symphony 1997: Heaven Earth Mankind
creator: tan-dun
type: Symphony with bianzhong, cello and children's choir
note: Tan Dun's symphony for the Hong Kong handover, using the replica bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng with Yo-Yo Ma.
description: Written for the ceremonies marking the return of Hong Kong to China in 1997, the symphony combines a symphony orchestra, a children's choir, solo cello played by Yo-Yo Ma, and a replica of the bianzhong of Marquis Yi of Zeng, the bells of the fifth century BC. Its three parts, Heaven, Earth and Mankind, quote Cantonese opera and folk song and pay tribute to Chinese history and the new era. The piece shows how the ancient bell set became a national symbol, and how Tan Dun bridges ancient sound and modern orchestra. It is still in copyright.
